lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the price system
lead.head: You can’t outlaw gravity

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 66

body: Amit Varma opened with a griev­ance against grav­ity, which makes Bengalis slouch. The state, he pro­posed, should use its co­er­cive power to out­law it.
Ajay Shah had a counter-offer: “Or I can write the gor­geous eco­nom­ics book, *Floating to Utopia*.” {066-J01}

The joke had a point. Supply and de­mand, Varma said, is a law of eco­nom­ics much like grav­ity. “You can no more make so­ci­ety bet­ter by mess­ing with prices than you can make us fly by cre­at­ing a law against grav­ity.”

Over the next hour the hosts took apart five ways gov­ern­ments med­dle with prices[[x1]]: price caps, rent con­trol, the min­i­mum wage, min­i­mum sup­port prices for crops and im­port tar­iffs. Each time, they ar­gued, it is the poor who pay.
## A mir­a­cle no­body planned

The case starts with Friedrich Hayek’s essay *The Use of Knowledge in Society*, writ­ten in the mid-1940s against the cen­tral plan­ners. Society, Hayek ar­gued, is too com­plex, and wants change too fast, for any­one to plan it from the top.

“How do peo­ple like you and me ful­fil the needs of peo­ple mil­lions of miles away who we don’t know, we will never meet, and yet we play a part in their hap­pi­ness?” Varma asked. “And the an­swer is prices.” {066-C01}

Prices carry in­for­ma­tion and in­cen­tives at once, Varma said. If a fire con­sumed a tenth of India’s tim­ber, he would learn of it from dearer pen­cils and fur­ni­ture, and economise, while grow­ers would be drawn in.
## Five ways to break it
Cap the price of a car at Rs 10,000, Varma said, and cars do not be­come af­ford­able. They van­ish into short­ages, queues and black mar­kets.

Rent con­trol, he said, is one rea­son build­ings on Bombay’s Marine Drive are di­lap­i­dated, with some ten­ants pay­ing around Rs 150 a month for flats that would oth­er­wise fetch four or five lakh.

A min­i­mum wage prices out any­one whose work is worth less than the floor. In India, Shah said, it is about Rs 13,000, against Rs 8,000 across the bor­der in Bangladesh, and India has one of the low­est em­ploy­ment rates in the world. {#wage}
Support prices tilted farm­ers to­wards ce­re­als and, in arid Punjab, to­wards rice, whose burnt stub­ble fouls Delhi’s air every year.

And a tar­iff qui­etly takes a few ru­pees from every con­sumer and hands them to an or­gan­ised lobby. Hence Varma’s Law: “Every in­ter­fer­ence in free mar­kets leads to a re­dis­tri­bu­tion of wealth from the poor to the rich.” {066-C13}
## The les­son that fades
Shah held up Europe as the model. When Putin cut off its gas, no­body capped the price. Supply surged, and gov­ern­ments paid poor house­holds di­rectly so they could af­ford the ex­pen­sive gas.
So why do politi­cians keep reach­ing for caps? Varma counted both Kamala Harris and Donald Trump, in the cur­rent US elec­tion, among the en­e­mies of the price sys­tem.

Shah called the for­get­ting a sorcerer’s ap­pren­tice prob­lem: peo­ple raised in pros­per­ity know that the sys­tem works but not why, and slip back into the in­stinct that the gov­ern­ment should fix things.

Political ma­tu­rity, Shah said, is the abil­ity to stom­ach large price fluc­tu­a­tions. “Wisdom lies in cre­at­ing a world of free­dom where prices fluc­tu­ate and then being quiet and doing noth­ing using state power when prices go up or prices go down.” {066-C08}

second.label: Cement and steel
second.head: A ministry in mourning
second.deck: Ajay Shah’s journalist friend watched officials grieve when price controls ended

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the ministry that mourned decontrol

body: In the early 1980s a jour­nal­ist friend of Ajay Shah’s cov­ered the ce­ment and steel min­istries, just as the gov­ern­ment abol­ished its price con­trols on both[[x2]].

Under the con­trols, Shah said, any­one who wanted to build had to bat­tle for ce­ment and steel, or ended up with sub­stan­dard ce­ment. He draws a di­rect line from it to build­ings of the 1950s and 1960s that later col­lapsed.

When de­con­trol was an­nounced, the whole gov­ern­ment build­ing felt a per­sonal catas­tro­phe: the mar­ket would now sort out ce­ment and steel, and no­body needed the of­fi­cials any more. {066-S01} As Shah put it, “in a sen­si­ble coun­try you don’t need a min­istry of steel, you don’t need a min­istry of ce­ment.” {#ministry}

quote.text: They had this aura of a catas­tro­phe like some fam­ily mem­ber has died.

third.head: Capped fare, missed flight

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the friend who missed his flight

body: Delhi once tried cap­ping Uber’s surge pric­ing[[x3]], Amit Varma said. A friend of his who knows eco­nom­ics well didn’t know about the cap, did not plan for the short­age, and missed his flight. {066-S03}

Varma’s thought ex­per­i­ment: 200 cabs serve 200 rid­ers, then sup­ply falls to 100. {#ubers} With surge pric­ing, the rider rush­ing to a hos­pi­tal or an air­port can out­bid some­one going out ca­su­ally.

The surge also reaches the idle driver. “You are sit­ting at a katta. Maybe if you’re Bengali, you’re going to have an af­ter­noon nap at that point,” Varma said. Seeing dou­ble the fare, he joins the sup­ply. {066-J06}
In the long run, an ap­pren­tice car­pen­ter might be­come a driver. Cap the fare and all three ef­fects switch off: the cabs go first come, first served.

box.title: The essay behind the episode
box.text: Friedrich Hayek’s *The Use of Knowledge in Society*[[x9]], writ­ten in the mid-1940s against the cen­tral plan­ners[[x10]], ar­gues that knowl­edge is too dis­persed for any­one to plan from the top. Amit Varma says he still often thinks of it, to re­mind him­self. {066-R02}

sections.label: The foundation
sections.head: No committee made this pencil
sections.caption: the miracle of prices
body: Friedrich Hayek wrote *The Use of Knowledge in Society* in the mid-1940s, Amit Varma said, as a reply to cen­tral plan­ners who be­lieved they could de­cide from the top how much of every good to make and what it should cost. Hayek later called that be­lief the fatal con­ceit[[x12]]. {066-R03}

Hayek’s an­swer was that the world is too com­plex. Millions of peo­ple “con­tain mul­ti­tudes”, Varma said, and their wants change from minute to minute. Only a de­cen­tralised sys­tem can cope, and that sys­tem has ex­isted for­ever: prices.

Leonard Read’s essay *I, Pencil*[[x11]] shows the mir­a­cle at work. A pen­cil comes out of the co­op­er­a­tion of peo­ple in forty coun­tries, felling tim­ber, ship­ping it, fit­ting the graphite, with no ge­nius and no com­mit­tee in charge. {#pencil}
## The re­source al­lo­ca­tion

Ajay Shah, ad­mit­ting that econ­o­mists are “very bad peo­ple” who turn or­di­nary words into jar­gon, called the whole ar­range­ment the re­source al­lo­ca­tion: a com­plete list of who must do what in an econ­omy. {066-J05}

Written down, Shah said, it would run to mil­lions of pages. Central plan­ning tries to write it, as Indian fi­nance still does through tens of thou­sands of pages of reg­u­la­tion. Markets dis­cover it in­stead.
~ “The only thing that crosses the cell wall of the firm is the price,” he said. “And all the magic of the mar­ket econ­omy hap­pens.” {066-C02}

quote.text: Prices act as both in­for­ma­tion and they act as in­cen­tives.

sections.label: Price caps
sections.head: Cheap cars, none for sale
sections.caption: price caps
body: Imagine, Amit Varma said, that a leader de­cides ev­ery­one should own a car, and caps the price at Rs 10,000[[x13]]. {#cars}
Ajay Shah asked lis­ten­ers to pause on the hor­ror of it: a law that uses state co­er­cion to pe­nalise a trans­ac­tion be­tween con­sent­ing adults at any other price.

The con­se­quences fol­low at once, Varma said. Cars stop sell­ing, and what stock ex­ists goes to the black mar­ket or to who­ever comes first. The cap does not make cars cheaper; it takes them out of ex­is­tence. {066-C04}
## The usual some­thing

Caps on air tick­ets after a nat­u­ral dis­as­ter, per­haps the Kerala floods, con­jure no new planes, he said. The seats go first come, first served, so a pas­sen­ger with a dire emer­gency may get noth­ing while a triv­ial trip goes ahead.
Nixon’s gaso­line cap in the 1970s OPEC cri­sis brought long queues at gas sta­tions. Venezuelans paid black-market prices for toi­let paper and milk. Soviet bread lines went around blocks.
Why do politi­cians keep at it? Varma quoted *Yes Minister*: “this is a prob­lem, we must do some­thing, this is some­thing, let’s do it.” The usual some­thing is a price cap. {066-J13}
~ In a com­pet­i­tive mar­ket, Varma said, ev­ery­thing is priced the way it is for a rea­son, and a fat profit mar­gin draws in new­com­ers until it sorts it­self out.

quote.text: You haven’t ac­tu­ally made a change in the price of the thing. You’ve just taken it out of ex­is­tence.

sections.label: Rent control
sections.head: Rent asunder
sections.caption: rent control
body: Amit Varma reached rent con­trol[[x14]] by way of a mon­de­green. For years he heard ‘Aabodana’, in a song from the 1970s film *Gharaonda* about being alone in the city in search of shel­ter, as ‘Sabudana’. {066-J08}

A gov­ern­ment sees vot­ers strug­gling with ris­ing rents and fixes the rent, so the land­lord can­not raise it. “The in­ten­tion is good and that is seen,” Varma said. “The con­se­quence is bad and that is un­seen.” {066-C09}

Landlords stop main­tain­ing their build­ings. Developers stop build­ing. Housing grows scarce, so ev­ery­thing out­side rent con­trol costs more. Over the years the property’s value falls to­wards noth­ing, which for the owner is theft.
## Where you sit

Varma and Ajay Shah both know a left­ist, a hard­core statist, who has lived for two gen­er­a­tions in a rent-controlled flat near Shivaji Park. Where you stand de­pends on where you sit, Varma said. {066-S06}

In an early episode of *The Seen and the Unseen*, the econ­o­mist Alex Tabarrok told Varma that the rent-controlled parts of New York looked like a bombed-out city. Varma re­called the dystopian film *Escape from New York*. {066-J15}
~ He also pointed to Michael Shellenberger’s *San Fransicko*, and to Hernando de Soto’s *The Mystery of Capital*: a prop­erty drained of its value by the state stops work­ing as cap­i­tal. {066-R14}

quote.text: He has been a life­long ben­e­fi­ciary of theft en­abled by the state.

sections.label: Minimum wage
sections.head: Priced out of a job
sections.caption: the minimum wage
body: Amit Varma once be­lieved a min­i­mum wage was how you pull a coun­try out of poverty. A Milton Friedman video changed his mind and sent him down a rab­bit hole of books and ar­ti­cles. {066-R15}

The logic is sim­ple, he said. Fix the min­i­mum at 100 and any­one whose work the mar­ket val­ues at 90 is priced out of a job. Thomas Leonard’s *Illiberal Reformers* shows that some pro­gres­sive labour laws of the first half of the twen­ti­eth cen­tury were meant to keep African Americans and women out of work.
## Both sides at once

In India, Ajay Shah said, the min­i­mum wage is about Rs 13,000[[x15]], while in com­pa­ra­ble Bangladesh the wage is Rs 8,000. Mandatory en­ti­tle­ments push the cost of hir­ing at the low­est lev­els to about Rs 17,000 a month. {#allin}

The same num­ber feeds NREGS pay­ments, which an­chor what work­ers ex­pect. So firms are kept from hir­ing and work­ers from ac­cept­ing, and India ends up with one of the world’s low­est em­ploy­ment rates[[x16]], below Bangladesh, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia.
Bangladesh, mean­while, rides a labour-intensive man­u­fac­tur­ing boom: those earn­ing 8,000 yes­ter­day earn 10,000 today, Varma said, and will earn 13,000 to­mor­row.
~ Shah backed KP Krishnan’s idea for break­ing the log­jam: free IT and IT-enabled ser­vices from labour law first, then ex­tend it to other in­dus­tries if it works. {066-R18}

quote.text: The al­ter­na­tive to a low wage job is not a high wage job. The al­ter­na­tive to a low wage job is no job.

sections.label: Import tariffs
sections.head: Ten rupees you never see
sections.caption: import tariffs
body: A local maker sells some­thing for Rs 100, Amit Varma said. A Chinese seller of­fers the same qual­ity[[x17]] for Rs 90. {#china}

The local mak­ers lobby, and the gov­ern­ment puts a tar­iff of Rs 20 on the Chinese good, which now costs Rs 110[[x18]]. The con­sumer buys local for Rs 100, pay­ing Rs 10 more with­out even know­ing it.

Those ten ru­pees, from every dis­persed con­sumer, would have gone into the econ­omy and cre­ated jobs. That is un­seen. What is seen is the local maker doing well. Gathered to­gether, the ru­pees go to an in­ter­est group: Varma’s Law in ac­tion. {066-C13}
## A game no­body lifts

Protection hurts the firm too, Varma said. Shielded from China on price and qual­ity, it need not lift its game. Exposed to the world, it would build bet­ter pro­cesses, the learn­ing would seep into the econ­omy, and it might even ex­port. {066-C14}
Ajay Shah added that trans­port, by con­tainer ship or by air, al­ready pro­tects do­mes­tic firms: get­ting goods to Bombay is eas­ier from Pune than from Mozambique.

~ Varma, by his own ac­count, hates tar­iffs, and said so im­po­litely. “If I’m trad­ing with some­one in China and we are hav­ing a dou­ble thank you mo­ment, what the F is anyone’s prob­lem?” he asked.

quote.text: Now the more com­pe­ti­tion there is, the more we have to lift our game, the harder we have to try

sections.label: Why we forget
sections.head: The sorcerer’s apprentices
sections.caption: generational amnesia
body: If peo­ple learn from their mis­takes, Amit Varma asked, why hasn’t pol­i­tics learnt its lessons? In the cur­rent US elec­tion, he said, Kamala Harris, with her talk of price goug­ing, and Donald Trump are both en­e­mies of the price sys­tem. {066-J19}

Ajay Shah re­called Angela Merkel’s line: Germany’s fu­ture would be known only when gen­er­a­tions with no mem­ory[[x19]] of the Second World War came of age and formed their own po­lit­i­cal phi­los­o­phy.

Economics, he said, has the same prob­lem. Hayek, Friedman and oth­ers won the ar­gu­ment, and a great age of pros­per­ity fol­lowed, but those raised in it lost the con­nec­tion with where they came from. {066-C15}
## Fall, di­ag­nose, re­peat

His work­ing hy­poth­e­sis is that every ten, twenty or thirty years, gov­ern­ments must try ac­tivism and fall flat, and there must be enough in­tel­lec­tu­al­ism around to di­ag­nose the fail­ure. Pensions show the dan­ger: twenty-five years on, the lessons have not been learnt. {#pensions}

Varma met the same am­ne­sia at a con­fer­ence on lib­er­al­ism in Washington, DC. Azar Nafisi, au­thor of *Reading Lolita in Tehran*, said lib­eral val­ues are voiced most truly by dis­senters in Iran, for whom it is an ex­is­ten­tial bat­tle. {066-S09}
~ Someone born in 2004, Varma said, never saw pre-liberalisation India or the Soviet Union. Hence his warn­ing: “the price of lib­erty has to be eter­nal vig­i­lance.” {066-J21}

quote.text: So it’s like a sorcerer’s ap­pren­tice prob­lem that this thing works, but you don’t know why it works.

There is a fur­nace that makes pros­per­ity, which is the mar­ket econ­omy. And then a gov­ern­ment may choose to tax that mar­ket econ­omy and use it for help­ing poor peo­ple through di­rect trans­fers, but you don’t in­ter­fere with the fur­nace.

p3.title: Price tales
p3.deck: Four stories of prices left alone, and prices meddled with

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Putin’s energy blackmail and Europe’s reply
stories.head: The squeeze that prices broke
body: When Putin in­vaded Ukraine, Ajay Shah said, he also tried en­ergy black­mail[[x20]]. Europe had im­pru­dently come to rely[[x21]] on Russian gas, and Putin hoped that by cut­ting the sup­ply he could break the Western coali­tion back­ing Ukraine.
The price of gas went “up to in­fin­ity”, Shah said. {#infinity} Russian pro­pa­ganda talked openly of Europeans freez­ing to death in their houses and com­ing back to beg.

Yet no­body in the European pol­icy space reached for price con­trols. {066-S04} On the de­mand side, the high price sorted users out: some fac­to­ries shut down, some switched to elec­tric­ity, and some paid up and kept run­ning.

On the sup­ply side, en­gi­neer­ing com­pa­nies built new LNG ter­mi­nals in no time. European buy­ers scoured the world and di­verted tankers out of Qatar that were bound for other coun­tries. And in the United States, where frack­ing and hor­i­zon­tal drilling had al­ready made the shale rev­o­lu­tion, gas pro­duc­tion and ex­ports surged.
“The sup­ply re­sponse only comes in re­sponse to the price,” Shah said. Interfere with a high price, and you in­ter­fere with the sup­ply re­sponse.

That left the poor. Governments knew that pro-Putin far-right par­ties could win over vot­ers freez­ing at home, so they made large on-budget pay­ments to poor peo­ple, who used them to buy the ex­pen­sive gas.

~ Nobody had ex­pected Europe to beat the black­mail. For Shah it was “one of the most per­fect sto­ries of how to do pub­lic pol­icy”. Amit Varma mar­velled that no com­mit­tee of Europe’s most im­por­tant peo­ple could have planned it: “all these so­lu­tions came from un­ex­pected places.”

quote.text: And I was fas­ci­nated and im­pressed that no­body but no­body in the European pol­icy space jumped to price con­trols as the an­swer.

stories.postscript: Pranay Kotasthane and Nitin Pai had voiced ex­actly this fear on *The Seen and the Unseen* when the war broke out, Varma re­called.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Europe’s gas crisis

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s bleeding-heart moment in a quake zone
stories.head: The last shop standing
body: As a col­lege stu­dent, Amit Varma spent three days in an am­bu­lance[[x22]] with para­medic friends, driv­ing through the earth­quake-hit parts of Maharashtra, Latur among them.

In one vil­lage, one side had fallen down en­tirely. On the other stood a sin­gle gro­cery store, and vil­lagers com­plained that it was charg­ing so much it should be out­lawed. “And my ini­tial thought was how dare they, these evil cap­i­tal­ists,” Varma said. “I used to read Marx in those days.” {066-S02}

Today he would let the price sys­tem work. High prices make it like­lier that sup­plies reach the vil­lage, and that house­holds economise: half a packet of bread in­stead of three, shared with the neigh­bour, the cost split.
~ In an emer­gency, he said, the gov­ern­ment should spend its own money on those af­fected by a dis­as­ter. Interfering with prices only cre­ates a huge prob­lem.
stories.why: A high price in a dis­as­ter is a sig­nal that pulls in sup­ply and stretches what is left. Compassion, in Varma’s telling, be­longs in the government’s own spend­ing, not in caps. Letting prices ad­just in real time, he said, is mirac­u­lous. {066-C06}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the grocery store after the earthquake

stories.kicker: Amit Varma traces Delhi’s smog to a price in Punjab
stories.head: Rice in Punjab, smoke in Delhi
body: Punjab is arid, Amit Varma said, and should not grow rice[[x23]], which needs a lot of water. But the gov­ern­ment an­nounced a min­i­mum sup­port price for rice[[x24]]. {066-S08}

So farm­ers used free farm elec­tric­ity, which mainly ben­e­fits rich farm­ers, to dig borewells and pump out ever more water. After the har­vest comes rice stub­ble, and the cheap­est way to be rid of it is to burn it.

“Every year at that par­tic­u­lar time of the year when the farm­ers of Punjab burn their rice stub­ble, a foul wind car­ries it to Delhi,” Varma said, and the city’s pol­lu­tion is then at its worst.
~ There is no po­lit­i­cal so­lu­tion, he said. The same party rules both states, but no­body can mess with the farm­ers, who will fight back tooth and nail.
stories.why: One dis­torted price set off a chain: de­pleted ground­wa­ter, burnt fields, foul air and po­lit­i­cal dead­lock. A price in­ter­ven­tion, Varma said, builds an equi­lib­rium that is ex­tremely dif­fi­cult to break out of, be­cause those who ben­e­fit fight back.
stories.postscript: Support prices for ce­re­als but not pulses, Varma re­called, meant more car­bo­hy­drates and less pro­tein in India: “a hu­man­i­tar­ian crime”. {066-S07}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Punjab’s rice and Delhi’s smog

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on rent control in Bombay
stories.head: Marine Drive, ₹150 a month
body: Walk along Marine Drive in Bombay, Amit Varma said, and you will often find build­ings that are old, di­lap­i­dated and not in great shape. He points to rent con­trol, which India started in 1949[[x25]], as one rea­son. {#rent-1949}
He hears of ten­ants pay­ing “ridicu­lous amounts like Rupees one fifty a month or what­ever”, for flats that would oth­er­wise rent for four or five lakh a month. {066-S05}

At such rents a land­lord has no rea­son to main­tain the build­ing, and no de­vel­oper has rea­son to build. “Would you build a build­ing in Marine Drive if your rent is going to be one fifty ru­pees or what­ever the hell it is?” Varma asked.
~ Housing grows scarce, and ev­ery­thing out­side rent con­trol costs more. These are not even un­in­tended con­se­quences, Varma said: eco­nomic the­ory pre­dicts ex­actly this.
stories.why: A tenant’s cheap rent is the seen ben­e­fit; a crum­bling build­ing, no new con­struc­tion and dearer flats for ev­ery­one else are the un­seen cost. For the land­lord, Varma said, rent con­trol is theft[[x26]]. {066-C09}

overheard.text: We’re talk­ing about prices and the show is free. Is it worth it?
overheard.who: Amit Varma, signing off an episode about prices

quiz.q: What did Amit Varma propose the state should outlaw, so that Bengalis would stop slouching?
quiz.a: Gravity, with an ap­pli­ca­tion for the ban to be writ­ten in trip­li­cate.

quiz.q: What, according to Varma’s Law, does every interference in free markets lead to?
quiz.a: A re­dis­tri­bu­tion of wealth from the poor to the rich, said Varma.

quiz.q: How did the cement and steel ministries react when price controls on both were abolished?
quiz.a: As if a fam­ily mem­ber had died: their im­por­tance was knocked out.

quiz.q: Why did a friend of Varma’s, who knows his economics, miss a flight in Delhi?
quiz.a: Uber surge pric­ing had been capped, and he didn’t know about it.

quiz.q: According to Ajay Shah, what is the alternative to a low-wage job?
quiz.a: Not a high-wage job, Shah said, but no job at all.

quiz.q: Where, according to Azar Nafisi, are classical liberal values expressed in their truest sense?
quiz.a: Among dis­senters in Iran, for whom it is an ex­is­ten­tial bat­tle.

glossary.def: A full spec­i­fi­ca­tion of who pro­duces what in an econ­omy
Coordination that emerges from many peo­ple but no one de­signed
Property that can­not work as cap­i­tal, in Hernando de Soto’s term
A mis­heard lyric, like Varma’s ‘Sabudana’ for ‘Aabodana’
A place to sit about idly, as Varma’s Uber driver does
Minimum sup­port price, a price the state guar­an­tees farm­ers for a crop

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 66. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Friedrich Hayek (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0); Richard Nixon (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Milton Friedman (Bachrach Studios, public domain); Angela Merkel (Armin Linnartz, CC BY-SA 3.0 de); Hernando de Soto (Institute for Liberty and Democracy, CC BY-SA 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: Four Papers That Changed the World (Episode 41)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts ex­plain land­mark pa­pers in plain lan­guage, no­tably Coase on why firms exist and Hayek on how prices co­or­di­nate a so­ci­ety no plan­ner can grasp.

shelf.title: The Use of Knowledge in Society
shelf.creator: Friedrich Hayek
shelf.why: Hayek’s ar­gu­ment that the knowl­edge needed to run an econ­omy is dis­persed among mil­lions of peo­ple, and that prices, not plan­ners, carry it: a lan­guage through which strangers tell each other what they want and lack.

shelf.title: The Fatal Conceit
shelf.creator: Friedrich Hayek
shelf.why: Hayek names the core error be­hind cen­tral plan­ning and price con­trols: the be­lief that any­one can know enough to run a com­plex so­ci­ety from the top down, when the knowl­edge it needs is spread across ev­ery­one.

shelf.title: I, Pencil
shelf.creator: Leonard Read
shelf.why: A pen­cil nar­rates its own mak­ing from ma­te­ri­als and know-how scat­tered across many coun­tries, co­or­di­nated by prices with no one in charge.

shelf.title: Price Controls Lead to Shortages and Harm the Poor
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s case that you can­not leg­is­late scarcity away: price caps dis­cour­age pro­duc­ers and in­no­va­tors, so goods don’t get cheaper but van­ish into short­ages and black mar­kets, hurt­ing the poor they claim to pro­tect.

shelf.title: Prices, Fast and Slow
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s piece, which Amit calls won­der­ful, on what hap­pens when the state messes with prices.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A five-and-a-half-hour mas­ter­class from Ajay on the war and the deep his­to­ries of Russia and Ukraine, built on a life­time of read­ing and a counter to Russian pro­pa­ganda.

shelf.title: The State of the Ukraine War (Episode 14)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mil­i­tary-strategy anal­y­sis of the war: how it is chang­ing the way wars are fought, Ukrainian in­no­va­tion, and its de­mo­graphic toll on Russia, from deaths to the flight of a mil­lion of its best and bright­est.

shelf.title: Russia, Ukraine, Foreign Policy (Episode 268 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane and Nitin Pai
shelf.why: Pranay Kotasthane and Nitin Pai on Europe’s dis­as­trous re­liance on Russian pipe­lines in­stead of di­ver­si­fy­ing sup­ply, and their fear, later borne out, that the gas de­pen­dence could be used as a weapon.

shelf.title: The Complete Yes Minister
shelf.why: Among the loveli­est and fun­ni­est books Ajay has read, with real in­sight into pol­i­tics and the dif­fi­culty of change; its satire of re­flex­ive pol­i­cy­mak­ing (‘we must do some­thing, this is something’) ex­plains why price caps are the de­fault po­lit­i­cal re­sponse.

shelf.title: Alone in the City
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It is where Amit first tied the search for a home in the city to the dam­age rent con­trol does.

shelf.title: Rent Control (Episode 14 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Alex Tabarrok
shelf.why: Alex Tabarrok’s short primer on the un­seen con­se­quences of rent con­trol, with the vivid case of rent-controlled New York look­ing like a bombed-out city.

shelf.title: San Fransicko
shelf.creator: Michael Shellenberger
shelf.why: Amit calls it a great book.

shelf.title: The Mystery of Capital
shelf.creator: Hernando De Soto
shelf.why: De Soto’s idea of ‘dead capital’: with­out prop­erty rights, un­ti­tled slum homes and re­stricted land are worth some­thing but can’t be bor­rowed against or in­vested, so the poor can’t turn what they own into cap­i­tal.

shelf.title: Milton Friedman on the minimum wage
shelf.creator: Milton Friedman
shelf.why: Friedman’s short video ar­gu­ment that a min­i­mum wage doesn’t lift a low-productivity worker’s pay to the legal floor: it makes the job il­le­gal, so the wage drops to zero.

shelf.title: Illiberal Reformers
shelf.creator: Thomas Leonard
shelf.why: It shows that some cel­e­brated pro­gres­sive labour leg­is­la­tion of the early 20th cen­tury was meant to keep African Americans and women out of the work­force.

shelf.title: Understanding India’s Pensions Disaster (Episode 65)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A first-principles ac­count of pen­sion re­form: how a small com­mu­nity with a shared phi­los­o­phy built the NPS, and how guar­an­tees and the old mess re­turned once that com­mu­nity dis­persed and its knowl­edge faded.

shelf.title: Snatching decline from the jaws of growth
shelf.creator: KP Krishnan
shelf.why: It pro­poses a prac­ti­cal wedge: fully dereg­u­late labour law in IT and IT-enabled ser­vices, where work­ers ob­vi­ously don’t need pa­ter­nal­is­tic pro­tec­tion, then ex­pand to other in­dus­tries if it works.

shelf.title: Stay Away From Luxury Beliefs (Episode 46)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: On be­liefs im­ported from rich-world dis­course that make their hold­ers feel vir­tu­ous while hurt­ing the peo­ple they claim to help, such as the min­i­mum wage, or op­pos­ing sweat­shops that beat every other op­tion work­ers have.

shelf.title: How to Do Development (Episode 57)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The case, built on Lant Pritchett’s ev­i­dence, that every human wel­fare in­di­ca­tor tracks per capita GDP, so sus­tained growth, not re­dis­tri­bu­tion or small solv­able projects, is the way out of poverty.

shelf.title: What’s Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Episode 18)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why Indian farm­ing, which em­ploys 40 to 60% of Indians against about 5% in rich coun­tries, is held back by the lack of a work­ing price sys­tem: MSPs that favour ce­re­als over pulses, loan waivers in­stead of struc­tural re­form, gluts and col­laps­ing prices.

shelf.title: The Great Redistribution
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s ar­gu­ment that mar­ket in­ter­ven­tions such as tar­iffs or bans on FDI in re­tail qui­etly move money from many dis­persed, poor con­sumers to a few or­gan­ised, rich in­ter­est groups, the op­po­site of their stated in­ten­tion.

shelf.title: Graduating to Globalisation (Episode 48)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s case that in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion is the en­gine of growth: com­pet­ing with the world forces firms to im­port best prac­tices and raise their game, and the gains spread through the econ­omy.

shelf.title: Reading Lolita in Tehran
shelf.creator: Azar Nafisi
shelf.why: Nafisi’s point, that lib­eral val­ues are voiced most truly by dis­senters in Iran, shows what gets lost when free so­ci­eties take lib­erty for granted.

shelf.title: Slouching Towards Utopia
shelf.creator: Bradford De Long
shelf.why: It gives a bet­ter struc­tural un­der­stand­ing of the old eco­nomic pol­icy con­sen­sus that ex­isted be­fore Trump, Putin, Xi Jinping and the right-wing au­thor­i­tar­i­ans.

shelf.title: Price Theory
shelf.creator: Milton Friedman
shelf.why: Some things were done right by the old mas­ters, and the best way to un­der­stand prices is to go back and study them.

shelf.title: Life Lessons
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit and Ajay’s course on what they wish they had been taught at twenty: learn­ing how to learn, frame­works for think­ing, writ­ing, prob­a­bilis­tic in­tu­ition, eco­nom­ics, the his­tory of thought, per­sonal fi­nance (Ajay’s mod­ule is ‘legendary’) and health.

laughs.text: Amit opens by blam­ing grav­ity for the Bengali ten­dency to slouch and pro­poses the state sim­ply ban it: ‘We should use the co­er­cive power of the state to out­law grav­ity... Can you please write an ap­pli­ca­tion for me in trip­li­cate?’ Ajay replies: ‘Or I can write the gor­geous eco­nom­ics book, Floating to Utopia.’
Amit on the body round­ness index, which Ajay had in­tro­duced him to a day or two ear­lier: ‘I think only to be able to cast a slur upon me with­out, you know, sound­ing rude.’

Amit’s Bengali read­ing of De Long’s title: ‘the urge for utopia is a dis­ease of the mind. But the slouch­ing is a prob­lem of the body.’ He re­turns to it at the close: ‘Slouching Towards Utopia to­tally em­bod­ies all Bengaliness.’
On what makes de­cen­tralised co­or­di­na­tion pos­si­ble: ‘today I’m sure there are tech bros who would say blockchain... But that mirac­u­lous tech­nol­ogy has ex­isted for­ever. It is prices.’
Ajay: ‘econ­o­mists are very bad peo­ple be­cause we re­pur­pose or­di­nary English words and endow them with spe­cial­ized tech­ni­cal mean­ings and then they are jar­gon.’
Amit on how surge pric­ing reaches the idle driver: ‘You are sit­ting at a katta. Maybe if you’re Bengali, you’re going to have an af­ter­noon nap at that point.’

Amit on se­lec­tive lib­er­tar­i­ans: ‘There will be one group of peo­ple who will be like two con­sent­ing adults can do what­ever they want in the bed­room, but not in the mar­ket­place. And an­other group which will say the op­po­site thing... Freedom is free­dom.’

Amit’s mon­de­green: for years he mis­heard ‘Aabodana’ in a song from the 1970s film Gharaonda, about being alone in the city search­ing for shel­ter, as ‘Sabudana’. He sets it up by ask­ing Ajay whether he loves sabu­dana khichdi and vada, adding ‘Full starch, by the way.’
Amit on Indian pol­i­tics: ‘every party is left wing on eco­nom­ics, every party is right wing on so­ci­ety, and they’re both anti free­dom, there­fore they’re anti free­dom in every mar­gin.’

Amit, un­char­ac­ter­is­ti­cally blunt: ‘I hate tar­iffs. I fuck­ing hate im­port tar­iffs... If I’m trad­ing with some­one in China and we are hav­ing a dou­ble thank you mo­ment, what the F is anyone’s prob­lem?’

Amit in­tro­duc­ing his clos­ing rec­om­men­da­tion, Prices, Fast and Slow: ‘It’s an ar­ti­cle writ­ten by a very good friend of mine. I don’t know if you’re aware of him. But your aware­ness of him may de­pend on your level of self aware­ness. Because this is Ajay Shah I’m talk­ing about.’
Yes Minister, via Amit: the politician’s in­stinct is ‘this is a prob­lem, we must do some­thing, this is some­thing, let’s do it’, and the usual ‘something’ is a price cap.

Amit’s list of price-cap fail­ures: Nixon’s gaso­line cap dur­ing the 1970s OPEC cri­sis and the long queues at gas sta­tions, Venezuelans pay­ing black-market prices for toi­let paper and milk, and Soviet bread lines that went around blocks.

Escape from New York: Amit men­tions this dystopian film while de­scrib­ing how rent-controlled parts of New York looked like a ‘bombed out city’, the image from his early Seen and the Unseen episode with Alex Tabarrok.
‘Where you stand de­pends on where you sit’: the old maxim Amit ap­plies to his statist friend in a rent-controlled flat.
Angela Merkel, quoted by Ajay: we will know Germany’s fu­ture only when gen­er­a­tions with no mem­ory of the Second World War come of age and form their own po­lit­i­cal phi­los­o­phy.
Bob Dylan, quoted by Amit when launch­ing Life Lessons: ‘he not busy being born is busy dying.’
